text: How is an AYUSH product registered in India? Ayurveda, Siddha and Unani (ASU) drugs are regulated primarily under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act 1940 and its Rules, administered by the Ministry of AYUSH together with State Licensing Authorities. To manufacture an ASU medicine you need: (1) a manufacturing licence from the State Drugs Controller / State Licensing Authority for ASU drugs; (2) compliance with Good Manufacturing Practices set out in Schedule T of the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, including suitable premises, equipment, and a qualified technical staff (an expert in the relevant system); (3) the product to be either a classical formulation from an authoritative textbook listed in the First Schedule, or a patent/proprietary ASU medicine whose formulation is based on those texts. Classical medicines do not need proof of efficacy but must follow the textual formula; patent or proprietary medicines require the label to state the reference to the ingredients from authoritative books. Registration/licensing is state-based, and separate licences are needed for manufacture, loan licence, and sale.

What is required to obtain an ASU drug manufacturing licence? A manufacturer of Ayurveda, Siddha or Unani (ASU) drugs must apply to the State Licensing Authority for ASU drugs. Key requirements under the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules include: adequate manufacturing premises and machinery meeting the Good Manufacturing Practices in Schedule T; qualified technical staff (for Ayurveda, a person holding a degree/diploma in Ayurveda recognised under law; corresponding qualifications for Siddha and Unani); proper documentation of the formulations to be made, distinguishing classical formulations (from First Schedule texts) from patent/proprietary formulations; and provision for quality testing, either in-house or through an approved laboratory. Licences are issued in prescribed forms (e.g. Form 25-D for manufacture of ASU drugs and Form 24-D for the application), are subject to inspection, and must be renewed periodically. Loan licences allow use of another licensee's approved premises.

What is the difference between classical and patent/proprietary ASU medicines? A classical (or generic) ASU medicine is one manufactured strictly according to the formulae described in the authoritative Ayurveda, Siddha or Unani texts listed in the First Schedule of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act (for example Charaka Samhita, Sushruta Samhita, Ashtanga Hridaya for Ayurveda). Because the formula and claims come from recognised texts, efficacy data is not separately required, but the product must faithfully follow the textual formulation and process. A patent or proprietary ASU medicine is a formulation developed by the manufacturer that is not a straight classical formula but whose ingredients are drawn from the authoritative books; its label must state the ingredients with reference to those texts, and it can carry a brand name. Patent/proprietary medicines may attract additional requirements such as safety/stability data, and their therapeutic claims are restricted to those consistent with the classical basis of the ingredients.

How does AYUSH regulation distinguish cosmetics from drugs? Under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, a 'drug' includes substances intended for use in diagnosis, treatment, mitigation or prevention of disease, whereas a 'cosmetic' is intended to be applied to the human body for cleansing, beautifying, promoting attractiveness or altering appearance, without therapeutic claims. The classification turns mainly on the claims made and the intended use. An Ayurvedic preparation marketed to cure or treat a condition (e.g. an anti-psoriasis oil, a medicated hair-fall treatment) is a drug and needs an ASU drug licence; the same botanical marketed only to cleanse or beautify (e.g. a herbal shampoo or moisturiser with no disease claim) is a cosmetic regulated as such and requires a cosmetic manufacturing licence. Making disease-treatment claims on a product licensed only as a cosmetic is a regulatory violation. Businesses must therefore match their claims to the correct licence category.

What quality standards apply to Ayurvedic products? ASU drugs must meet quality standards set through the pharmacopoeial framework and Good Manufacturing Practices. The Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India (API), Siddha Pharmacopoeia and Unani Pharmacopoeia, published under the Pharmacopoeia Commission for Indian Medicine and Homoeopathy (PCIM&H), lay down identity, purity and strength standards, tests and assay methods for single drugs and formulations. Manufacturers must comply with Good Manufacturing Practices in Schedule T of the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules covering premises, equipment, hygiene, raw-material authentication, in-process controls, finished-product testing and record keeping. Products must observe limits for heavy metals (lead, mercury, arsenic, cadmium), microbial contamination, pesticide residues and aflatoxins, especially for export. Proper labelling (batch number, manufacturing/expiry dates, licence number, ingredients with textual reference) is mandatory. Metal-based (bhasma/rasa) preparations have additional safety and standardisation expectations.

What regulations apply to exporting AYUSH products? Export of Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani and Homoeopathy products is promoted by the Ministry of AYUSH and facilitated through bodies such as PHARMEXCIL (Pharmaceuticals Export Promotion Council). Exporters generally need: a valid ASU drug manufacturing licence; compliance with the importing country's regulatory category (many countries treat these as food/dietary supplements, herbal medicines, or traditional medicinal products rather than licensed drugs); and quality documentation. Commonly required certificates include a Certificate of Pharmaceutical Product (CoPP) or Free Sale Certificate, GMP certificate, and heavy-metal / contaminant test reports, since limits on lead, mercury, arsenic and cadmium are strict abroad. Labelling and claims must conform to the destination market's rules (e.g. EU Traditional Herbal Medicinal Products Directive, US dietary-supplement DSHEA rules). Exporters should also ensure Access and Benefit Sharing / NBA compliance where Indian biological resources are involved.

Are clinical trials required for AYUSH medicines? For classical ASU formulations made strictly per First Schedule texts, separate clinical efficacy trials are generally not mandated, as safety and efficacy are presumed from long traditional use. However, for patent or proprietary ASU medicines making specific therapeutic claims, and particularly for new interventions or metallic/mineral preparations, the AYUSH regulatory framework and the amended Drugs and Cosmetics Rules require appropriate safety, toxicity and, where claims warrant, clinical data. Research is overseen with reference to Good Clinical Practice guidelines for ASU medicine and ethics-committee approval. The Central Council for Research in Ayurvedic Sciences (CCRAS) and sister councils conduct and standardise such research. Manufacturers introducing genuinely novel formulations or health claims should expect to substantiate safety and, for the claim, efficacy, whereas straightforward classical products rely on textual authority.

What must appear on the label of an ASU medicine? The Drugs and Cosmetics Rules prescribe labelling for Ayurveda, Siddha and Unani medicines. The label must show: the name of the drug; whether it is a classical or a patent/proprietary medicine; for patent/proprietary medicines, the true list of all ingredients with quantities and the reference to the authoritative text from which they are drawn; the name and address of the manufacturer and the manufacturing licence number; the batch or lot number; the date of manufacture and date of expiry; net content; directions for use and dosage; and the words indicating the system (Ayurvedic/Siddha/Unani medicine). Claims must be restricted to those supported by the classical basis of the ingredients, and exaggerated or misleading disease-cure claims are prohibited (also under the Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisements) Act 1954). Cautionary statements are required for schedule-restricted or metallic preparations.

What intellectual property options exist for an AYUSH innovator? An innovator working with Ayurveda, Siddha or Unani has several IP routes, chosen by what is being protected. A genuinely novel, non-obvious and industrially applicable formulation, process, extraction method or device may be patentable - but not if it is merely a known traditional-knowledge aggregation (barred by Section 3(p) of the Patents Act) or is anticipated by TKDL prior art. A distinctive brand name (e.g. Chyawanprash brand names, Dabur, Patanjali) is best protected by a Trademark, renewable indefinitely. Confidential formulations that cannot be reverse-engineered and need no disclosure may be kept as Trade Secrets. Original written material, monographs and artwork attract Copyright. A region-linked traditional product (e.g. a herb tied to a locality) may qualify for a Geographical Indication. Often the best strategy combines a trademark on the brand with a patent only on the genuinely novel element, while respecting ABS obligations for the biological resources used.

section: Role of the Ministry of AYUSH and CCRAS
text: What is the role of the Ministry of AYUSH and CCRAS? The Ministry of AYUSH (Ayurveda, Yoga & Naturopathy, Unani, Siddha, Sowa-Rigpa and Homoeopathy), formed in 2014, is the central body for policy, education, research, standardisation, quality control and promotion of these systems, and it co-owns the TKDL with CSIR. It works with regulatory and pharmacopoeial bodies (PCIM&H) and export promotion councils. The Central Council for Research in Ayurvedic Sciences (CCRAS) is the apex body for research in Ayurveda, undertaking drug standardisation, safety and clinical studies, and documentation - and it also files patents on validated innovations (for example CCRAS has been granted patents on standardised Ayurvedic interventions). For an innovator or manufacturer, these institutions provide pharmacopoeial standards, research validation, standard treatment references, and policy guidance that underpin both regulatory licensing and IP strategy for AYUSH products.
